title: Four retrieval opportunities
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton maps out the four places in a maths course where teachers can build in retrieval practice and weighs the main pros and cons of each. The Do Now builds a settling routine and covers many topics but wastes time if students fake effort; the low-stakes quiz allows longer and equipment-based questions but eats curriculum time; weaving old topics into the current unit shows how maths connects but is impossible for some pairings; and homework costs no lesson time but gives the teacher little control over who actually retrieves. The framing is useful because it treats retrieval as a scheduling problem with trade-offs rather than a single technique, inviting a department to use a mix. The closing section is a plug for Eedi's free retrieval system, which is a minor part of the post.
points: Four retrieval slots are available to teachers: the Do Now, the low-stakes quiz, weaving into the current topic, and homework, each with distinct strengths.
The Do Now and quiz differ in coverage and seriousness: the Do Now covers many concepts and sets a routine, while the quiz suits topics needing protractors, compasses or calculators.
Weaving past topics into new units makes retrieval feel less like a bolt-on, but some topic pairings simply cannot be woven.
Homework is the only option that does not use lesson time, yet the students who most need retrieval practice are often those who skip it.
quotes: You will struggle to find a teacher who does not believe that giving students opportunities to revisit concepts they have studied in the past is important to prevent them from forgetting what they once knew.
When done regularly, this can form part of a routine that settles students and sets them up for success for the rest of the lesson. You can also cover many concepts each week.

The longer time compared to a Do Now not only means more topics can be covered, but also topics that require specialist equipment such as protractors, compasses and calculators. Students may also take this more seriously than a Do Now.
This feels less of a bolt-on than retrieval during the Do Now and Low-Stakes Quiz, helping students see the interconnected nature of mathematics.
It is tricky to weave in certain topics. Try weaving in rotations into a unit on cumulative frequency diagrams, or simultaneous equations into a lesson on percentage increase.
This is the only retrieval opportunity that does not take up precious lesson time. As a result, students can spend as long as they need on any given question.
Teachers have less knowledge about who has done the retrieving. And the simple fact is that many students - often the ones we most need to do retrieval - do not do their homework.
